A broker replies within one working day.", "content": "", "template": null, "parent": null, "order": 6 }, { "slug": "property-business-interruption", "title": "Property and business interruption", "excerpt": "Cover for your buildings, contents and stock, and for the profit you would lose while the business recovers.", "content": "

A fire, flood or break-in damages more than a building. This cover pays to repair or replace what was lost and keeps the business funded while it gets back on its feet.

Request a property quote
Call a broker

What it covers

  • Buildings at full rebuild cost, including demolition and professional fees
  • Contents, machinery and stock, including stock in transit or at other sites
  • Business interruption: lost gross profit and the extra cost of trading during repairs
  • Loss of rent if you let all or part of the property
  • Optional extras such as equipment breakdown, terrorism and denial of access

Who it suits

  • Firms that own or lease their premises
  • Manufacturers with specialised machinery and long lead times
  • Landlords with commercial or mixed-use buildings
  • Businesses holding stock of significant value

What affects the price

  • Rebuild value and construction type
  • Fire and security protection, such as alarms and sprinklers
  • Flood exposure and claims history
  • The length of the indemnity period you choose

An illustrative example

A joinery workshop has an electrical fire overnight. Property cover pays to repair the unit and replace two CNC machines. Business interruption pays the profit lost during the fourteen months it takes to source the machines and win back two contracts, plus the cost of renting a temporary unit.

A hypothetical scenario to show how the cover works. Not a real client or claim.

Common questions

What is an indemnity period?

The length of time business interruption cover will pay for after a loss. It should cover a realistic rebuild and recovery, which is often 18 to 24 months rather than 12.

What happens if I am under-insured?

Most policies apply average: if you insure for 70% of the true value, a claim may be reduced to 70%. We check declared values with you at every renewal.

Is flood cover included?

Usually, but not always, and it may carry a higher excess in flood risk areas. Your recommendation report will say so clearly.

", "template": "page-service", "parent": "services", "order": 0 }, { "slug": "liability-insurance", "title": "Liability insurance", "excerpt": "Employers', public and products liability, plus professional indemnity for firms that give advice or design.", "content": "

If an employee, customer or member of the public holds your business responsible for an injury, damage or financial loss, liability insurance pays for your defence and any compensation.

Request a liability quote
Call a broker

What it covers

  • Employers' liability, a legal requirement for most UK employers
  • Public liability for injury or damage to other people at your premises or on site
  • Products liability for goods you make, supply, repair or import
  • Professional indemnity for claims that your advice, design or service caused a loss
  • Legal defence costs, including representation in health and safety prosecutions

Who it suits

  • Any business with employees
  • Contractors who must meet limits set in main contracts
  • Manufacturers, importers and distributors of products
  • Consultants, designers and other advisory firms

What affects the price

  • Turnover, wage roll and the type of work you do
  • Where your products are sold, especially North America
  • Health and safety procedures and training records
  • The limit of indemnity your contracts require

An illustrative example

A shopfitter's employee drops a panel that injures a visitor at a client's store. The visitor claims for the injury and lost earnings. Public liability pays the defence costs and the settlement, and the policy meets the indemnity clause in the shopfitting contract.

A hypothetical scenario to show how the cover works. Not a real client or claim.

Common questions

How much public liability cover do I need?

Often your contracts decide. Limits of 2, 5 and 10 million pounds are common. We read the clause with you and match the cover to it.

Do I need employers' liability for part-time staff?

In most cases, yes. It applies to part-time, temporary and casual staff too. There are narrow exemptions, for example some family businesses.

Does professional indemnity cover past work?

Professional indemnity is written on a claims-made basis, so it responds to claims made while the policy is active, including for past work, provided cover has been continuous.

", "template": "page-service", "parent": "services", "order": 1 }, { "slug": "cyber-insurance", "title": "Cyber insurance", "excerpt": "Incident response, data restoration, lost income and payment fraud, with help preparing for the questions insurers ask.", "content": "

Most cyber incidents at smaller firms start with an email. Cyber insurance pays specialists to contain the attack and restore your systems, and covers the income you lose while you are offline.

Request a cyber quote
Call a broker

What it covers

  • Incident response: a 24-hour helpline, IT forensics and legal advice
  • Data and system restoration after ransomware or a failed attack
  • Business interruption while your systems are down
  • Liability and regulatory costs if personal data is exposed
  • Payment fraud, where staff are tricked into paying a fake invoice (often with a lower limit, so check it)

Who it suits

  • Firms that hold customer or employee personal data
  • Businesses that take payments or send invoices by email
  • Companies that cannot trade when their systems go down
  • Suppliers whose contracts require cyber cover

What affects the price

  • Multi-factor authentication on email and remote access
  • Offline backups, and how often you test a restore
  • Turnover and the volume of personal data you hold
  • Patching, staff training and past incidents

An illustrative example

An accountancy practice opens an attachment that appears to come from a client, and ransomware encrypts the file server. The insurer's response team isolates the network, restores data from backups and handles notifications to clients. The policy pays their fees and three days of lost billing.

A hypothetical scenario to show how the cover works. Not a real client or claim.

Common questions

Do insurers pay ransoms?

Cover for ransom payments varies and some insurers exclude it. Most claims are resolved by restoring from backups, which is why insurers ask so much about them.

We are a small firm. Are we really a target?

Most attacks are automated and indiscriminate. Smaller firms are often hit because they have fewer controls, not because anyone chose them.

What if we do not have multi-factor authentication?

Many insurers will not quote without it. We can tell you which controls matter most and help you close the gaps before renewal.

", "template": "page-service", "parent": "services", "order": 2 } ], "posts": [ { "title": "What business interruption cover actually pays for", "cat": "guides", "date": "2026-09-29 09:00:00", "image": "cover-interruption", "excerpt": "Business interruption keeps a company trading after a fire or flood. It is also the cover most often set too low.", "content": "

Business interruption cover replaces the gross profit you lose while your premises or equipment are being repaired, and pays the extra costs of keeping customers served in the meantime. It sits alongside your property policy: if there is no valid property claim, there is usually no interruption claim either.

The sum insured is a forecast, not last year's figure

Policies ask for a gross profit figure for the indemnity period. That should be what you expect to earn over the length of a realistic rebuild, including growth, not what appears in last year's accounts.

Pick an indemnity period that matches reality

Twelve months is common and often too short. Planning permission, specialist machinery and supply chain delays can push recovery to eighteen or twenty-four months.

  • Check lead times for your most specialised equipment
  • Ask how long it would take to win back a lost customer
  • Include time to recruit and train staff

If you are unsure, ask your broker to run a simple loss scenario with you before renewal.

" }, { "title": "Cyber cover: the questions insurers ask before they quote", "cat": "cyber", "date": "2026-10-06 09:00:00", "image": "cover-cyber", "excerpt": "Cyber underwriters now ask detailed questions about your security controls. Having the answers ready makes quoting faster and often cheaper.", "content": "

Cyber insurance pays for incident response, data restoration, notification costs and lost income after an attack. Before quoting, most insurers want to understand the controls you already have in place.

Expect questions on these controls

  • Multi-factor authentication on email and remote access
  • Offline or immutable backups, and how often you test a restore
  • How quickly you patch critical vulnerabilities
  • Staff training on phishing and payment fraud

Missing one of these does not always mean a decline, but it can mean higher premiums or exclusions. Fixing the gaps before renewal is often the best value improvement you can make.

Read the payment fraud section carefully

Losses where staff are tricked into paying a fake invoice are sometimes excluded or carry a low limit. Ask for the limit to be shown clearly in your quote.

" }, { "title": "Renewal season: preparing your schedule six weeks out", "cat": "renewals", "date": "2026-10-13 09:00:00", "image": "cover-renewal", "excerpt": "A good renewal starts well before the invitation arrives. Six weeks gives your broker time to test the market properly.", "content": "

Insurers price risks they understand. The clearer your renewal information, the more insurers will quote and the stronger your negotiating position.

What to send your broker

  • Updated turnover, wage roll and staff numbers
  • Changes to premises, sites or stock values
  • New products, services, contracts or countries you trade in
  • Any claims or incidents in the past year, even small ones

Review the values, not just the price

Rebuild costs and equipment prices have moved a lot in recent years. If buildings or contents are under-insured, a claim can be reduced in proportion, so check the declared values at every renewal.
